title: Ezekiel 43:1–12
context: The guide brings the prophet to the east gate, and the glory of the God of Israel comes from the way of the east, with a voice like the sound of many waters and the earth shining with his glory. The prophet says it was like the vision he saw when he came to destroy the city and like the vision by the river Chebar, and he falls on his face. The glory enters the house by the east gate, and the Spirit brings the prophet into the inner court, where the LORD’s glory fills the house. Earlier the glory had gone out from over the threshold and stood over the cherubim (10:18), then to the east gate of the LORD’s house (10:19), and then gone up from the city to stand on the mountain on the east side of the city (11:22–23). Now it returns “from the way of the east.” The LORD then speaks from the house, calling it the place of his throne, where he will dwell among Israel forever, and he calls for the defilements of the past to be put away. The prophet is to show the house to Israel so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities and keep its law. Both traditions read the return of the glory as shared ground about the LORD’s faithfulness to dwell with his people.

verses.text: Afterward he brought me to the gate, even the gate that looks toward the east.
verses.arminianNotes: Afterward he brought me to the gate, Arminian readers see the prophet brought to the very gate where the glory had paused before departing (10:19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the guide leads the prophet to the east gate deliberately. The setting prepares for the reversal of the departure described in chapters 10-11.

verses.text: Behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the east. His voice was like the sound of many waters; and the earth was illuminated with his glory.
verses.arminianNotes: Behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the east. Arminian readers picture the glory returning from the direction in which it had gone, toward the mountain on the east side of the city (11:23).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare the sound of many waters with 1:24, where the wings sounded like the noise of great waters, named without merging the scenes. The earth shining with his glory shows the LORD’s majesty.

verses.text: It was like the appearance of the vision which I saw, even according to the vision that I saw when I came to destroy the city; and the visions were like the vision that I saw by the river Chebar; and I fell on my face.
verses.arminianNotes: It was like the appearance of the vision which I saw, Arminian readers see the prophet linking this vision to the earlier ones, the vision when he came to destroy the city and the vision by the river Chebar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the vision of destruction is usually taken as chapters 8-11 and the vision by the Chebar as chapter 1. The prophet falls on his face as in 1:28, and the visions are named side by side.

verses.text: The LORD’s glory came into the house by the way of the gate which faces toward the east.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s glory came into the house by the way of the gate which faces toward the east. Arminian readers find the departure reversed: the glory that left by the east gate now returns by it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 44:1-2 later says the east gate is shut because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it. Both traditions read the return as the LORD’s faithfulness to his promise.

verses.text: The Spirit took me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the LORD’s glory filled the house.
verses.arminianNotes: The Spirit took me up and brought me into the inner court; Arminian readers see the climax of the return: the LORD’s glory filled the house, as the cloud once filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare 1 Kings 8:11, where the LORD’s glory filled the LORD’s house at its dedication, and 10:4, where the house was filled with the cloud before the departure. Each scene stands in its own setting.

verses.text: I heard one speaking to me out of the house, and a man stood by me.
verses.arminianNotes: I heard one speaking to me out of the house, and a man stood by me. Arminian readers distinguish the voice from the house, the LORD himself, from the guide who stands beside the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the voice from the house speaks in the first person as the LORD in 43:7. The guiding man remains present but is not the one who speaks.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell among the children of Israel forever. The house of Israel will no more defile my holy name, neither they nor their kings, by their prostitution and by the dead bodies of their kings in their high places;
verses.arminianNotes: Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet. Arminian readers see the LORD promising to dwell among the children of Israel forever, shared ground for both traditions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s dwelling as shared ground; compare 37:26-28, Jeremiah 3:17, and Revelation 21:3. The royal corpses mentioned here are read either as actual burials or as memorial monuments, and the text does not settle it.

verses.text: in their setting of their threshold by my threshold and their door post beside my door post. There was a wall between me and them; and they have defiled my holy name by their abominations which they have committed. Therefore I have consumed them in my anger.
verses.arminianNotes: in their setting of their threshold by my threshold and their door post beside my door post. Arminian readers see the problem of royal buildings placed so close to the LORD’s house that only a wall divided them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the nearness of palace and temple appears to have blurred the line between the holy and the common. The LORD names this as defiling his holy name, the reason for his anger.

verses.text: Now let them put away their prostitution, and the dead bodies of their kings far from me. Then I will dwell among them forever.
verses.arminianNotes: Now let them put away their prostitution, and the dead bodies of their kings far from me. Arminian readers see a call to remove what defiled the LORD’s dwelling, joined to his promise: Then I will dwell among them forever.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some connect the royal burials with the garden of Uzza (2 Kings 21:18, 26), though the link is uncertain. Both traditions read the verse soberly as a call to holiness.

verses.text: “You, son of man, show the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities; and let them measure the pattern.
verses.arminianNotes: You, son of man, show the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities; Arminian readers see the vision of the house given to lead the people to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that shame here is the fruit of seeing God’s holiness, compare 16:61-63 and 36:31-32. Shame leading to repentance is largely shared ground between the traditions.

verses.text: If they are ashamed of all that they have done, make known to them the form of the house, its fashion, its exits, its entrances, its structure, all its ordinances, all its forms, and all its laws; and write it in their sight, that they may keep the whole form of it, and all its ordinances, and do them.
verses.arminianNotes: If they are ashamed of all that they have done, make known to them the form of the house, Arminian readers recognize the fuller revelation given to those who respond with true shame over their sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the list of the house’s form, fashion, exits, entrances, structure, ordinances, forms, and laws. The vision is to be written in their sight so that they may keep it and do it.

verses.text: “This is the law of the house. On the top of the mountain the whole limit around it shall be most holy. Behold, this is the law of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: This is the law of the house. Arminian readers see the whole limit around the top of the mountain declared most holy, holiness extending beyond the inner sanctuary to the entire area.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same declaration frames the verse at both ends. The holiness once confined to the most holy place now marks the whole mountain.
